query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of Al2O3 ceramic particles into a refractory high‐entropy alloy will lead to in-situ formation of fine TiO precipitates that enhance high-temperature yield strength via precipitation strengthening while maintaining room-temperature ductility and reducing overall alloy density compared to the alloy without oxide addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 or TaNbVTi-based alloy) produced by powder metallurgy methods without any oxide additions, exhibiting dislocation‐mediated plasticity.
generation.intervention: Introduce a specific percentage (e.g., 15 wt% optimized from prior studies) of Al2O3 ceramic particles during ball-milling and spark plasma sintering to encourage in-situ formation of TiO precipitates.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective under high-temperature loading conditions (e.g., tensile or compressive tests conducted between 673 K and 873 K) while preserving performance at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formed fine TiO precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion, refining the microstructure and contributing to precipitation strengthening, while the low density of Al2O3 limits the overall alloy density.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 addition reacts during sintering to form finely dispersed TiO precipitates that impede dislocation motion at high temperatures, thus enhancing yield strength. Simultaneously, the ductile matrix is preserved at room temperature and the alloy density is reduced owing to the low-density ceramic phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have an approximately 30% higher yield strength at high temperatures (673–873 K), reduced density by nearly 15%, and comparable room-temperature ductility.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys processed without the addition of Al2O3, which rely primarily on solid solution and dislocation slip mechanisms with higher density.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is limited to the processing method involving powder metallurgy (ball-milling and spark plasma sintering) and within the high-temperature range of 673–873 K. Effects outside these conditions or in alternative alloy systems may vary, and long-term cyclic performance under actual turbine conditions remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: While similar systems have shown improved strength and reduced density with oxide additions, uncertainty remains regarding the stability of TiO precipitates at even higher temperatures and under prolonged operational cycles typical in jet-turbine service.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys using identical powder metallurgy processing: one set with a defined percentage (e.g., 15 wt%) of Al2O3 added and one without any oxide addition. Perform comparative mechanical tests at room temperature and in the high-temperature range (673–873 K), and conduct detailed microstructural analysis to assess precipitate formation.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM analysis for precipitate size and dispersion)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al2O3-added alloy fails to show at least a 30% increase in high-temperature yield strength along with a reduction in density and without compromising room-temperature ductility, or if the expected TiO precipitates are not observed, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). ## Abstract
AbstractA series of novel lightweight TaNbVTi-based refractory high entropy alloys (RHEA) were fabricated through ball-milling and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The reinforced phase of TiO precipitates were in-situ formed due to the introduction of Al2O3 ceramic particles. The RHEA with 15% Al2O3 exhibits a high compressive yield strength (1837 MPa) and a low density (7.75 g/cm3) with an adequate ductility retention. The yield strength and density are 32% higher and 15% lower, respectively, compared to the RHEA without Al2O3 addition. The specific yield strength (237 MPa cm3/g) of the RHEAs is much higher than that of other reported RHEAs, and is mainly ascribed to the introduction of high volume fraction of Al2O3 additives, resulting in solid solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening.
